video_title: The Bond Market “Crash” Is a Trap — AI Agents Are About to Ignite Crypto
gist: Jordi Visser argues the global long-bond selloff is a head-fake trade — bond vol, junk spreads and inflation swaps show no stress and governments are actively capping yields — while equities sit at the cheapest PEG since the late 1990s on rising revisions. His central thesis: AI has crossed from chatbots to agent swarms, agents need native digital money, and that convergence makes crypto and tokenization the highest-payoff asset class, with AI-hardware names 'stuck in the mud' until after the midterms.

insights.claim: The long-end yield selloff is not a credit event: bond volatility is sitting at low levels, junk spreads are at the tightest level ever, and inflation swaps across 1-, 2-, 5- and 10-year tenors all cluster at roughly 2.48-2.52%, the same level as core CPI.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Cross-asset confirmation is missing, so fading the bond-panic narrative (staying long risk) has better odds than positioning for a yield-driven crash; watch bond vol and junk spreads as the actual tripwires.
insights.quote: junk spreads wouldn't be sitting at the tightest level ever

insights.claim: The realized damage from the 2026 bond selloff is trivial versus the real bond bear market: 20-year-plus Treasuries are down about 3% in total return this year versus down 32% in 2022.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Sizing the actual drawdown shows the 'bond crash' is a headline, not a portfolio event — it argues against paying up for duration hedges or de-risking equities on rate fear.
insights.quote: your return this year minus 3%. Here's what it was in 2022 when it actually mattered, down 32%

insights.claim: The Japanese government bond scare has been a costly distraction: 30-year JGB yields have risen only about 117 basis points since breaking out to all-time highs in May of last year, while the Nikkei is up 52% year-over-year — meaning traders who acted on 'the biggest bond market is imploding' headlines missed roughly a 70% rally.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A concrete precedent that rising sovereign yields have coexisted with equity melt-ups — use JGB/Nikkei as the template rather than assuming yields cap stocks.
insights.quote: Here's where the Nikkei is year-over-year, up 52%. So, if you listen to this garbage, you cost yourself a 70% rally

insights.claim: The bond selloff is global (Japan, Germany, US, UK, Switzerland), driven by debt levels plus good growth rather than inflation, and governments will intervene to prevent it from becoming a crisis.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, citing Robin Brooks
insights.so_what: If the policy reaction function is 'cap yields', the pain trade is short duration into intervention; positions should be sized for official pushback, not a free-running yield spiral.
insights.quote: It won't spin out of control into a crisis because governments won't let it.

insights.claim: Yield suppression is being coordinated internationally, with the US Treasury Secretary publicly signaling he expects Japan to act to boost the yen and stating the two countries are in coordination — and the yen strengthened this week.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Coordinated FX/rate management is an underpriced constraint on the short-duration and long-dollar trades; a stronger yen alongside capped US yields supports risk assets.
insights.quote: Besson expects Japan to act to boost yen. We saw the yen again this week. Strengthen. I know what the Japanese are planning to do, says Bessant. We're in coordination.

insights.claim: Even a 25 basis point Fed hike is an insufficient reason to avoid equities while earnings and profit margins are still expanding, and the upcoming Fed meeting is a setup where a rally after a hike would confirm the uptrend.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Price action after the Fed — not the decision itself — is the tradable signal; a hike that the market absorbs is a green light to add risk.
insights.quote: The Fed meeting has now taken on extreme importance because if the market trades higher after the Fed raises rates, I don't think it's going to stop from that point.

insights.claim: Credit spreads should still widen at the low-quality end — triple-C spreads are already widening — because AI disruption will put a lot of companies out of business, even as index-level junk spreads sit at record tights.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A quality-dispersion trade inside credit: short the lowest tier of high yield against tight index spreads rather than betting on a systemic credit event.

insights.claim: The S&P 500 PEG ratio is at its lowest level since 1998 because forward earnings growth is running above the forward multiple, which contradicts the claim that the index is expensive.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Valuation-based bear cases have to argue that the growth rate itself collapses — that reframes the bubble debate onto earnings revisions, which are currently rising.
insights.quote: This is at the lowest level since 198. You cannot say that the market is expensive and it's a bubble

insights.claim: The strength is global, not just American: MSCI World is up 16% year-over-year, MSCI Emerging Markets up 30%, and the MSCI World Bank Index up 29% — and banks would not lead if there were a genuine bond or credit problem.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Bank relative performance is the cleanest live tell for a credit/bond crisis; while banks lead, treat rate-driven bear cases as noise.

insights.claim: Macro breadth confirms no recession signal: manufacturing PMI at 55, the Johnson Redbook five-week year-over-year average at 9.6% with consumption at 67% of the US economy, and the sixth-forward oil contract up 22% year-over-year at around $86.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: These are the weekly-to-monthly series to track for the first genuine crack; rising oil here reads as demand strength rather than a stagflation tax.

insights.claim: The tech-momentum unwind was mechanical deleveraging and short-covering rather than an earnings problem, so it should not be read as the start of a fundamental drawdown.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Positioning-driven drawdowns mean-revert; buying the momentum unwind is a different bet than buying a fundamentally broken tape.
insights.quote: This is about the long side going up and deleveraging continue to happen. That is what caused this.

insights.claim: A falling average true range percent across a 100-name AI thematic basket is a rarely used bottoming signal because it shows hedge funds are no longer being stopped out and retail speculation has left, and that measure has been declining every week.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A replicable indicator: track basket-level 14-day ATR% as a forced-selling gauge, with declining ATR% marking the exhaustion of stop-driven downside.
insights.quote: This thing is going lower. This is a very positive sign because this means hedge funds are not getting stopped anymore.

themes.theme: AI Trade Economics and Circular Finance

insights.claim: Interest rates barely matter to AI economics: a 10% decline in model prices costs roughly three percentage points of margin, while a 200 basis point rise in 10-year yields costs only about one margin point — so rates are a rounding error on inference P&L.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: This kills the 'higher rates pop the AI trade' thesis and reframes the true risk variable as model price compression — the metric to monitor is revenue per token, not the yield curve.
insights.quote: Interest rates are a rounding error on inference P&L.

insights.claim: In a concentrated economy the three companies that matter most are Anthropic, OpenAI and Nvidia, because Nvidia sells the chips to the model labs whose compute demand funds the rest of the hardware complex including Dell, Marvell and Micron.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Monitor the two private labs' pricing power as the upstream variable for the entire listed semiconductor and server complex — the chain breaks at model pricing, not at any single hardware name.
insights.quote: the three companies that matter are Anthropic, OpenAI, and Nvidia

insights.claim: Nvidia approaching new all-time highs while the SMH sits below a downtrending 50-day moving average is a bullish divergence, since every chip stock ultimately follows Nvidia as the payer at the center of the circular AI finance chain.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Use Nvidia's relative strength as the lead indicator to fade semiconductor bubble calls; the invalidation is Nvidia breaking down, not SMH weakness.
insights.quote: if their stock is breaking out, do you really want to call semiconductors a bubble?

insights.claim: AI infrastructure demand is still being revised upward, with Dell rising 9% on results and now guiding AI server revenue to triple versus an expectation of only doubling six months earlier, while countries such as Germany are running short of AI compute.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Guidance revisions of that magnitude support the capex cycle continuing; sovereign compute shortages point to a durable non-US demand leg.
insights.quote: The computer maker now sees AI server revenue tripling. Six months ago, it expected it only to double.

insights.claim: AI hardware names are 'stuck in the mud' and unlikely to make major new highs until after the midterm elections, with a name like Micron plausibly doubling within a year but no longer offering the ten-times payoff that has already been captured.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Argues for rotating capital out of AI hardware into higher-convexity exposure while holding a base position for the eventual post-midterm re-rating.
insights.quote: Do I think it'll double between now and the and next year? Probably. But a doubles not 10 times. That trade has already happened.

themes.theme: Agent Swarms and the AGI Threshold

insights.claim: Frontier models have gone from roughly 40% to essentially 100% on benchmarks measuring the ability to perform knowledge-worker jobs in about a year, which is why the current model release is being framed as the AGI threshold even though rollout will lag capability.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Capability saturation on knowledge-work benchmarks makes labor-cost deflation and white-collar disruption an investable multi-year theme well before headline job losses appear.
insights.quote: About a year ago, I think we were around the 40% level. We're now at 100.

insights.claim: The defining shift is agents operating in coordinated teams of about 1,200, with some agents sacrificing their own goals for the collective — which changes the mental model from AI assistant to AI organization.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: If the unit of AI is an organization rather than a tool, compute demand and the need for machine-native payments both scale far beyond current assistant-based forecasts.
insights.quote: they're working in teams of 1,200 to accomplish a goal. That's where we are now with the swarm.

insights.claim: Enterprises whose entire AI plan is buying seats of a chatbot for employees are already falling behind, because the competitive edge has moved to redesigning workflows around agents rather than distributing tools.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Seat-based AI adoption metrics overstate real enterprise progress; the differentiator to underwrite is workflow redesign, favoring AI-native companies over incumbents buying licenses.
insights.quote: If your major plan is to give everyone Anthropic, you are falling behind. That's not a joke. That is a reality.

insights.claim: OpenAI and Anthropic are signaling that the coming year will deliver as much AI progress as the previous four years combined — the span that took the field from ChatGPT to autonomous agents.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A compressed capability timeline pulls forward both the compute-demand curve and the disruption of incumbent service businesses.
insights.quote: the next year will be worth four years of AI progress

insights.claim: Crypto's mass-market use case never lacked a use case, it lacked a native user, and AI agents supply it — agents need stablecoins, digital payments and tokenization, which is the 'grand unification' of AI and crypto.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser, citing Marc Andreessen
insights.so_what: The core investable thesis of the episode: underwrite crypto infrastructure on agent transaction volume rather than on retail adoption cycles.
insights.quote: Crypto didn't lack a use case. It lacked a native user. AI creates it.

insights.claim: Bitcoin is the purest AI hedge because AI destroys existing businesses and replaces them with tiny five-to-ten person companies, making Bitcoin the index of the agent economy the way the S&P 500 indexes the US economy.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Reframes Bitcoin as an equity-disruption hedge rather than an inflation hedge, which changes what it should be paired against in a portfolio.
insights.quote: It's why I say Bitcoin is the purest AI hedge. It works because AI destroys all businesses.

insights.claim: Agent-to-commerce integrations are already shipping weekly, with Grok adding the ability to buy or lend crypto via a payments integration and Grokbot able to purchase goods on the internet through Stripe's Link.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Concrete, datable evidence that agentic payments are live — the leading indicator to track for the crypto transaction-volume thesis.
insights.quote: X's AI tool, Grock, now allows users to buy or lend crypto with Moonay integration.

insights.claim: The 'double debasement' thesis holds that AI compresses S&P multiples by changing terminal values while governments simultaneously debase currency to keep rates down and manage a K-shaped economy, so crypto takes a high percentage share of fiat assets over the next five years.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A structural allocation argument for crypto that does not require a macro crisis — it requires only continued policy suppression of yields plus AI-driven equity terminal-value uncertainty.
insights.quote: Crypto is going to take a high percentage of the fiat asset over the course of the next five years

insights.claim: Tokenized equities are already live at scale: Robinhood was upgraded by multiple firms partly on its new layer-2 chain, and stock token trading did about $1.5 billion of volume in just six weeks, with the growth curve resembling early AI token expansion.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Tokenized-equity volume is a measurable adoption series, and brokerages building chains are the listed way to express the tokenization theme.
insights.quote: In just six weeks, a billion a half dollars trades sounded like science fiction two years ago.

insights.claim: The real-world-asset market has grown 18 times, but phase one has been mostly tokenized money market fund collateral from firms like BlackRock and Franklin Templeton — phase two moves into tokenized stocks and even tokenized sports-team equity.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Distinguishing collateral tokenization from asset tokenization tells you which part of the RWA growth is already priced and which is the next leg.

insights.claim: The Clarity Act matters not for legality but for capital access — it gives pension funds and insurance companies the regulatory seal of approval to allocate, and its passage would trigger an immediate next leg higher in crypto.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A specific binary catalyst to position around; the risk case is an administration change reversing regulatory progress rather than the bill failing outright.
insights.quote: All Clarity does is give the regulation and basically the seal of approval for pension funds

insights.claim: Perpetual futures on private companies are a live financial innovation, with perps now existing on names like SpaceX and Anthropic, offering 24/7/365 trading and no futures roll.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Perps on private assets open a new venue for expressing views on unlisted AI companies and create a fresh source of crypto-rail transaction volume.

insights.claim: Quarter-to-date crypto has massively outperformed equities — Ethereum up 56%, Solana up 38%, Bitcoin up 36%, against the S&P 500 up 3%, the NASDAQ down 3% and semiconductors down 14%.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Quantifies the tracking-error risk for institutions with zero crypto exposure, which itself becomes a source of chase demand.
insights.quote: Ethereum up 56% quarter to date. Salana up 38. Bitcoin up 36. The S&P 500 up three, NASDAQ down three, SMH down 14.

insights.claim: The 'silent IPO' thesis is that long-time crypto ideologues have reduced or bailed out in frustration while most other investors missed the move waiting for an October bottom that is unlikely to arrive, leaving positioning unusually light into an uptrend.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Light positioning plus a rising 200-day is the setup for a chase; the absence of enthusiasm is the bullish variable, not a warning.
insights.quote: Most people believe this was going to bottom in October. It seems to be getting away. I don't think you're going to get the chance.

insights.claim: Position size should equal your subjective probability that the AI-agent thesis plays out — a 5% belief warrants a 5% allocation, a 10% belief warrants 10% — with the stop being a break of the prior lows and re-entry only above the 200-day moving average.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A concrete, repeatable allocation and risk rule that turns a thematic view into an actual sized trade with a defined exit.
insights.quote: If you think there's a 5% chance, you should have 5% of your money in it in my opinion.

insights.claim: Trades should be handicapped like horse races — look for value rather than the winner and sit out races with no edge — and Bitcoin currently reads as a 100-to-1 payoff that requires only a small stake to matter.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Convexity framing means the asymmetric payoff, not conviction in the outcome, justifies the position — a small allocation is the disciplined expression.
insights.quote: he told me to not look for the winner. Always look for value. If there is no edge in the race, sit it out.

insights.claim: The crowd sets the odds and mispricing appears where the crowd misses something — today the people holding most of the world's money neither use AI nor believe in crypto, which is precisely the pre-consensus stage where great trades begin.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Frames institutional non-adoption as the opportunity rather than the risk, and implies the trade degrades once allocators arrive.
insights.quote: Great trade start before consensus.
